Foreign Policy in the American Heartland: Issues for the 120th Congress

Commentary
by

Victor Cha,

Nicholas Szechenyi,
and
Gregory B. Poling

Published November 12, 2026

Following last week’s midterm elections, the 120th Congress will be sworn in on January 3. As the U.S. government determines foreign policy priorities for the next two years, members of Congress on both sides of the aisle will be looking ahead to the 2028 presidential elections. The preferences of swing-state voters in U.S. elections could determine the future direction of American foreign policy and grand strategy, perhaps more so than any other group of voters in the country. In partnership with Polity Research Consulting LLC, CSIS conducted a survey on U.S. foreign policy with a total sample of 1,000 registered voters across seven battleground states—Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin—engaging with a representative mix of independents, Democrats, and Republicans.* The authors are not aware of another systematic poll conducted on foreign policy attitudes among voters in these critical states. The survey found that voters across the political spectrum see strong connections between foreign policy and their daily lives. They disapprove of tariffs, they support international trade, and they prefer a United States that is engaged and leading in global affairs.

FINDING ONERespondents feel the impact of foreign policy.  There is an ongoing debate across the United States and among politicians over whether the country should be globally engaged or should focus first on America. That debate has no clear answer. However, CSIS’s survey showed that many registered voters think that global events really do affect their lives. Overall, 62 percent of respondents in the battleground states surveyed believe that developments outside the United States impact their daily lives a great deal or a fair amount. 

Remote Visualization

The survey asked an open-ended question about how that impact manifests in people’s lives. The most frequently cited impacts related to the cost of living, including rising energy costs, and the impacts of tariffs. A sample of the top responses has been coded as listed below.

FINDING TWORespondents want the United States to protect its allies and partners and advance democratic values. CSIS also wanted to know what registered voters in battleground states think about the United States’ role in the world. Amid narratives of scaling back U.S. obligations globally, a significant majority of respondents (94 percent) said U.S. allies and partners are very important or somewhat important to the United States. Likewise, a significant majority (85 percent) also said it was very important or somewhat important to protect democracy and human rights worldwide.  

Remote Visualization

Remote Visualization

FINDING THREERespondents oppose the war with Iran and tariffs. The survey asked swing-state voters their opinions on some of the major international developments of the past year. Of those voters, 56 percent oppose the war with Iran, and 55 percent are against tariffs.

Remote Visualization

Remote Visualization

FINDING FOURRespondents believe supporting Ukraine’s ability to defend itself remains in the national interest. Moreover, 77 percent believe it is very important or somewhat important to U.S. national security interests for Ukraine to have the ability to defend itself. A higher share of Democrats—51 percent—feel it is very important, compared to 38 percent of independents and 32 percent of Republicans. 

Remote Visualization

Remote Visualization

FINDING FIVEPartisan differences on key issues are limited. The survey found that swing-state independents, Democrats, and Republicans are aligned on a range of foreign policy issues. For example, at least 75 percent of respondents from all three groups believe that trade with other countries is good or somewhat good for the United States. Likewise, a significant majority of those surveyed consider it very important or somewhat important for the United States to fulfill its mutual defense commitments. 

Remote Visualization

Remote Visualization

FINDING SIXMost respondents view China as a military and economic threat. CSIS also wanted to better understand views on China, as the U.S.-China relationship is the most consequential bilateral relationship in the world.

Remote Visualization

A majority of respondents in the battleground states surveyed view China as an economic and military threat to the United States. Some—11 percent—think that a military conflict between the United States and China is inevitable.  

Remote Visualization

A plurality favor trade with China but with restrictions on sensitive technologies. These results suggest a general preference among swing-state voters for a tough but calibrated approach to managing U.S.-China relations. 

Remote Visualization

For more analysis on these topline results, go to CSIS.org. In the coming weeks, we will be releasing more detailed analysis of the survey results. 

*On behalf of the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), Polity Research Consulting LLC conducted 1,000 web-based interviews with registered voters across seven key swing states in the 2026 mid-term elections from September 10-17, 2026. The states surveyed were: Pennsylvania (N=191); Georgia (N=169); Michigan (N=167); North Carolina (N=164); Wisconsin (N=116); Arizona (N=97); and Nevada (N=96). Respondents were screened at the top of the survey for: being registered to vote in their state, being 18 years of age or older, and their gender identity. To ensure the representativeness of the sample, quotas were set for the number of voters sampled in each state, political party breakdowns within each state, and gender identity for the overall sample. The margin of error on the entire 1,000-member sample was ± 3.1 percent at the midrange of the 95 percent confidence interval.
